newsitem.title: USA: New SEC rule eases securities offering restrictions.
newsitem.headline: New SEC rule eases securities offering restrictions.

text.p: The Securities and Exchange Commission Wednesday adopted new rules that ease restrictions against securities issuers and underwriters, but retain the agency's broad powers to catch manipulators.
SEC officials said the rules were the most sweeping changes in regulations -- many of them outdated and burdensome -- that have been on the books for more than 40 years.

Known as Regulation M, the new rules seek to sharpen the way the SEC deals with potential manipulation by issuers, bond or share holders and underwriters who might artificially raise the market price of a security under distribution, thus boosting its offering price.
But in doing so, the SEC said the rules were crafted to ease regulatory burdens and costs for underwriters and issuers.

Trading by underwriters and issuers in actively traded securities -- those with an average daily trading volume of $1 million or more and whose issuers have a public float of at least $150 million -- would not be restricted, it said.
This would eliminate restrictions on equity securities of about 1,900 domestic issuers and many foreign issuers, said Richard Lindsey, the SEC's market regulation chief.
"What this means for firms and their trading desks ... is greater simplicity, greater ease and facility in handling underwriting practices," said SEC Chairman Arthur Levitt.

He and other SEC officials said the new rule will not diminish protection for investors as the agency will continue to use its broad powers to bring fraud lawsuits against those manipulating securities offerings.
Lindsey said while the rules reduce prohibitions on trading during an offering, exchanges will be relied on to sharpen surveillance to detect any manipulation quickly.
Other features of the new regulations:
-- The period of trading restrictions for most securities would be reduced to one or five business days, from the current two or nine business days, depending on type of security.

-- Trading restrictions on derivatives during an offering of the associated security would be eliminated. Trading restrictions on the associated security would be imposed, however, when its derivative security is distributed.
-- Transactions in most debt, preferred and asset-backed securities would be deregulated.
-- The SEC will expand the availability of Nasdaq "passive" market-making during distributions of Nasdaq securities.
-- It will reduce the regulated period for short-sales in connection with a public offering.

In other actions, the SEC proposed for public comment rules to carry out provisions of a law enacted earlier this year that delineates federal and state securities regulatory functions and gives the SEC more powers to regulate the mutual fund industry.

Under a provision that seeks to free from regulation certain private mutual funds owned by highly sophisticated investors, or "qualified purchasers," the SEC proposed to define the type of investments required to be called such.
The agency also put out for public comment its proposals on how investment advisers may determine whether they should be regulated by the SEC or by state regulators.
